->Introduction of Porphyry<-

# CONCERNING

the knowledge which appears clearly useful for the sake of philosophizing, specifically regarding the teaching of those five <note>Referring to the "Five Voices" (quinque voces) or "Universals" of Porphyry: Genus, Difference, Species, Property, and Accident.</note>: to know what is <term>Genus</term> <note>original: "ser" (սեռ) - a general category or kind</note>, and what is <term>Difference</term> <note>original: "tarberut‘yun" (տարբերութիւն) - the specific trait that distinguishes one species from another within a genus</note>; what is <term>Species</term> <note>original: "tesak" (տեսակ) - a subdivision of a genus</note>, what is <term>Property</term> <note>original: "yatuk" (յատուկ) - a characteristic belonging exclusively to a certain species</note>, and what is <term>Accident</term> <note>original: "patahum" (պատահումն) - a non-essential quality that can change without the thing losing its identity</note>. This study will be beneficial for the clarification of definitions and altogether for the utility of demonstrations and examples. I shall deliver these to you by providing a concise tradition as an introductory handbook.

<summary>This page contains a 16th-century table of contents in French and the opening of the Armenian translation of Porphyry's "Isagoge." It introduces the fundamental logical concepts—the five universals—used in medieval philosophy to define and categorize the world.</summary>
<keywords>Porphyry, David the Invincible, Aristotle, Isagoge, Logic, Universals, Genus, Species, Armenian Philosophy, Scholasticism</keywords>

<meta>This page transitions from the general introductory headings of the previous page into the specific text of Porphyry’s "Isagoge" (Introduction to Logic), as translated and commented upon by the 6th-century Armenian philosopher David the Invincible. The text begins with the classic "Porphyrian questions" regarding the nature of universals.</meta>

As for the modes of signification, I shall pass over them briefly in speech, moving from the lower concepts to the higher, and encountering the simpler ones in due measure. I shall proceed with haste concerning **genus** <term>genus: the general category, such as 'Animal'</term> and **species** <term>species: the specific kind within a genus, such as 'Human'</term>. First, [it is asked] whether genus and species 

<margin>only</margin>

exist solely as thoughts of the mind, or if they are substantial—whether they are bodies or incorporeal—and whether they are separate from [sensible things] or exist within them. Regarding these profound matters, I shall refrain from speaking more deeply <note>The author is following Porphyry's famous refusal to solve the 'Problem of Universals' in an introductory text, as it is too advanced for beginners.</note>, for such an undertaking requires a different and greater inquiry. But now, concerning these, I shall speak of them in a more evident manner, laying hold of the logical path before me, and I will attempt to explain it to you simply. Concerning Genus.

<margin>What is said for now is tentative</margin>

And since it appears that I am not ignorant of what genus and species are, it is said that "man" is [an example]. Every care is taken to reach a similar conclusion. According to this, the **Heraclidae** <note>original: "կերակղեանցն" — the descendants of the Greek hero Heracles.</note> are called a "genus" [or race] from a single origin. And this is defined as the multitude of Heracles—those who possess the kinship and the sign of descent from other called genera. But "genus" is also spoken of in another way: as the beginning of each person’s birth, either from the parent or...

<column-break/>

...the one who begat them, even where they are no longer present. For in this way, we say that someone is "spoken of" as having a genus, and they keep their ancestry. And again, [one speaks] of this age, as if the genus were in being, and **Plato the Athenian** <note>The famous Greek philosopher.</note> [is said to have] the province from which he came as his origin; for each lineage is as the parent. But it appeared that their house remained standing, for the Heraclidae are named after the one called **Heracles**, and having established the house and the land, they were "of Heracles," and were his close kin. But "genus" was first named as the origin of each person's birth, and after this, the multitude [descending] from a single beginning—for instance, from Heracles—while distinguishing him from all others. And we call the whole completion of the Heraclidae a "genus." And "genus" is also spoken of in another way, under which the species is ranked, perhaps according to the similarity of these as stated. And since this is a kind of beginning for those who contemplate these things, it prepares a multitude [of concepts] under the given terms. But one must observe the "genus" spoken of according to the third [meaning] among **philosophers** <term>philosophers: literally 'wisdom-lovers' (իմաստասէրք)</term>, which the Word and others have explained, saying what a "genus" truly is.

<summary>This page introduces the logical concepts of genus and species, posing fundamental questions about whether these categories exist in reality or only in the mind. It provides common definitions of 'genus' as a lineage or place of origin, citing Heracles and Plato as examples, before moving toward a formal philosophical definition.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical definition of "Genus" from the previous page, contrasting it with other logical categories like "Species," "Property," and "Accident." The text is a translation of Porphyry's *Isagoge*, the standard introduction to Aristotelian logic in the Middle Ages.</meta>

...[it is said] of many things that differ in **species** <term>species: the sub-category within a genus, like 'Human' within 'Animal'</term>, [and it is] predicated in the category of "What is it?" For as for "animal," <gloss>is</gloss> it is predicated of those things which are under it. There are some things said of a single thing only, such as individuals—for instance, Socrates, or "this one" or "that one." But there are others [said] of many, such as [genera], and even the primary **differences** <term>difference: the characteristic that distinguishes one species from another, like 'rationality'</term>, and the common **properties** <term>property: a quality that belongs to all members of a species and only that species, like 'capable of laughter'</term> and **accidents** <term>accident: a quality that can change without the thing losing its identity, like 'being black' or 'sitting'</term> in a general sense, but not specifically to any one person. 
For instance, "animal" is a genus, and "man" is a species. There is also **difference**, which is restrictive; and **property**, for example, "the laughter-capable"; and **accident**, such as "white" or "black," and so on.
Now, the **genera** <term>plural of genus</term> differ from those things predicated of one thing only, because the genus is predicated of many things by its very definition, according to many species. 
As for the **species**, although it is predicated of many things, it is not predicated of those that differ in species, but rather of those that differ in number. For "man" is a species of which Socrates and Plato are predicated; these do not differ in species, but only in number. 
However, "animal," being a **genus**, is predicated of man, horse, and so on, which differ from one another in species and not merely in number.

<column-break/>

[The genus is] alone [predicated in this way]. And regarding the phrase "of those that differ":
For the **property** is predicated of only one species, and is equal to that species in its scope. 
For example, "laughter-capable" <gloss>is</gloss> predicated of man alone, and of all individual men. But the **genus** is not predicated of only one species, but of many things that differ in species. 
And the genus is distinguished from the **differences** and from the **accidents** in this way:
Even though differences and common accidents are predicated of many things that differ in species, they are not predicated in the category of "What is it?" 
If we are asked about the thing of which these are predicated, we are more likely to answer "of what sort" they are. For when asking "What sort of thing is a man?" we say "rational." And "What sort of thing is a crow?" we say "black." 
"Rational" is a **difference**, while "black" is an **accident**. 
But when we ask "What is a man?" we answer "an animal." Thus, "animal" is the **genus** of man. 
Therefore, by saying "of many things," 
<margin>property</margin>
we distinguish the genus from those things that are predicated of only one individual...

<summary>This page defines the logical "Genus" by contrasting it with individuals, species, properties, and accidents. It explains that a Genus answers the question "What is it?" (e.g., Man is an Animal) rather than "What sort is it?" (e.g., Man is Rational).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical definitions from Porphyry’s Isagoge, shifting from the definition of "Genus" to the definition of "Species" (Armenian: տեսակ, *tesak*). The text explains how these terms function within the "kingdom of thought" and introduces the "Tree of Porphyry," a hierarchical diagram used to organize all reality from the most general categories to specific individuals.</meta>

...be named. In the beginning, he distinguishes **species** <term>species: a sub-category that falls under a genus</term> from those [other categories], as if they were predicated of essences <note>original: էյուտեակաց (*ēut‘eakac‘*), meaning beings or essential entities</note> or as if they stood in their own right. In the inner animate soul, he explains [species] by distinguishing them from **differences** and from those things that occur **commonly** <term>accident: a non-essential quality, like being "tall" or "tan"</term>. To be precise, [he explains] what the others are within the essence, what kind they are, or how they possess **predication** <term>predication: the act of saying something about a subject, e.g., "The cat (subject) is black (predicate)"</term>. Therefore, the **genus** contains neither more nor less [than required]; these are the boundaries of the kingdom of thought.

---

**Species** is also said of each of the forms <gloss>forms</gloss> <note>The Armenian *tesak* translates the Greek *eidos*, which means both "species" and "visual form/shape"</note> according to which it is called a "primary form," worthy of [study] <gloss>affection/grace</gloss>. And **species** is also said of that which is explained under a **genus**; just as we are accustomed to saying that "man" is a species of "animal," and "white" is a species of "color," and "triangle" is a species of "shape." 

And when we defined species, we remembered to say: it is predicated of many things that differ in species <note>The text here clarifies that "Species" is what identifies "what a thing is" for many individuals</note> in the category of "What is it?" And when we speak of the **species**, we must know that it is that which is under the explained **genus**. For the genus is spoken of over the species. Each of the [two]— <note>The word is split here for the column break</note>

<column-break/>

—each of the two must necessarily be treated by those who discuss these matters using both aspects. Now, the definition of **species** is turned back toward the **genus**: a species is that of which the genus is predicated in its essence. And thus, species is predicated of many and of differing [individuals] according to "what they are" in their animate essence. 

But this definition belongs to the **most specific** <term>infima species: the lowest species in a hierarchy that cannot be divided into further sub-species, only individuals</term> which is the species alone. Others will necessarily follow the most specific. Let what is being said be observed from this: these modes of **predication** are themselves "most specific," and again others are "most generic." Between the **most generic** <term>summum genus: the highest category, such as "Substance," which has no genus above it</term> and the **most specific**, he looks at the relationship. 

The **most generic** is that above which there will be no other superior genus. The **most specific** is that below which there will be no other descending species. Between the most generic and the most specific, there are those which are both **genera and species** at the same time; however, they are called by different names depending on the direction. 

Let what has been said be established upon a single line of predication:
**Substance** is a genus.
Under it is **Body**.
Under Body is **Animate Body** <note>Meaning a living physical form</note>.
Under that is **Animal**.
Under Animal is **Rational Animal**.
Under which is **Man**.
And under Man is **Socrates**, as well as other individual humans.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Porphyry's Isagoge, specifically illustrating the "Tree of Porphyry." This is a hierarchical structure that maps reality from the most general category (Substance) down to the most specific individuals (like Socrates or Plato). The text explains how a single category can be both a species of the thing above it and a genus for the thing below it.</meta>

<margin>Of the likeness of quality, specific to that [species]</margin>
Now, of these, **Substance** <term>Substance: the most basic category of being that exists in itself, like 'a tree' or 'a man' rather than a quality like 'green'</term> is the most generic, and it alone is a genus [only]. And **Body** is a species of substance, and also a genus of the non-divine <note>In this logical system, "non-divine" refers to material or corporeal things as opposed to spiritual essences</note>; but the **Animate Body** is a species of body and a genus of **Animal**. Again, animal is a species of animate body, and also the genus of rational animals <gloss>man</gloss> and irrational animals <gloss>beast</gloss>, being the genus of man. And **Man** is a species of <gloss>rational</gloss> <gloss>immortal</gloss> and animal; but man is no longer called the genus of individual men, but only a species. And all the first individuals are called a species in a proximate way, as is the genus. <insert>within which is also substance</insert> being most natural. Nothing comes before these most particular ones; thus man is a species, after which there is no other species. And nothing from those things cut into species can be [further] individuals of others; for Socrates and Plato are mixed [within it], it is only a species. And the "last species," as we said previously at the beginning, is that which is before those individuals, which are species, and after them are the genera. Therefore, in these things, they have two compositions: from here, before them, according to which they are called species, and from here, after them, according to which

<column-break/>

their genera are named. But the extremes remain in their positions; for the **most generic** <term>genus generalissimum: the highest category that cannot be a species of anything else</term>, as if it holds the definition under which it is positioned, being a genus because it is supreme. But as it is [viewed] toward those below it, it is not mixed with the higher things that come first. And the former [species] is a single position, as if before that which is a species; but toward those after it, they have a different effect. Indeed, it is also called the species of the lower things, and the boundary of the individuals, as if containing them. Also a species again from them. <gloss>it divides the contained species from the genus, being distinct from the genus</gloss> and in this way: just as its species [stands] entirely. Whatever else might be a transcended genus. And the **most specific** <term>species specialissima: the lowest species that cannot be divided into further sub-species, only into individuals</term> which, being a species, is no longer a genus; and being a species, we shall not divide it into further species.
And furthermore: from the many and different things you learn what the predicates are, while the middle terms are called species and genera by their relationship to the extremes. And each of them is a species and a genus, but taken in different respects. But the first ones from the most specific, moving upward to the most generic, are called genera and also species. Two in one, like **Adam** and **Enoch**; **Sophroniscus** and **Peleus**, son of Peleus. <note>Sophroniscus was the father of Socrates; Peleus was the father of Achilles. These are standard classical examples of how individuals are grouped by lineage.</note> Likened to these, even as the "Race of Aram," <note>The translator uses 'Aram' to refer to the Armenian people, substituting the traditional Greek example of the 'Heraclidae' (descendants of Hercules) with an Armenian ancestor</note> yet they hold these genealogies in their minds.

<summary>This page describes the hierarchy of being, known as the Tree of Porphyry, moving from the "most generic" category of Substance down to the "most specific" category of Man, ending with individual people.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Porphyry's *Isagoge*, moving from the definition of the "Tree of Porphyry" to the specific philosophical problem of whether "Being" itself can be a single genus. It contrasts the views of Aristotle and Plato regarding the classification of reality from the most general categories down to the infinite number of individuals.</meta>

Having taken the beginning from this point many times: but as for that which is the master of forms and **Species** <term>Species: a specific group of things that share a common nature, located under a Genus</term>, it is not so. For **Being** <note>original: "էակն" (eakn) - existence or that which is</note> is not a common genus for all things in one single way. Nor are all things under one highest **Genus** <term>Genus: a broad category or "family" that contains several species</term> as Aristotle says. Instead, it is mentioned as in the first book of *Categories*: there are **ten genera**, which are the primary subordinate principles. 

And although he called all of them "beings," he says they are called so in a certain way and not equivocally <note>original: "փաղաքանակի" - likely referring to synonymous vs homonymous predication</note>. For if Being were one common genus for all things, then all beings would not be distinct in their predication. Rather, they share a commonality in name only, but not in the definition (the *logos*) of that name.

However, those we encounter as the **Most Generic** and the **Most Specific** are two distinct types, but they are not found in all things. As for the individuals that follow after the most specific species, Plato commands us to stop there. He suggests that while striving to divide through the intermediate stages—dividing the intermediates into species-making differences—one should let the "infinite" <note>the infinite number of individuals like specific people or objects</note> go. For there can be no certain knowledge or science of these infinite individuals. By descending to the most specific species, one must divide them

<column-break/>

continually. But with the most specific species, it is necessary to encompass the plurality. For the **Species** is one unchanging nature for a multitude in one place. Thus, a name is established. 

But according to the parts and the proper members, they are opposites; they become divided into a multitude. Just as among useless fish there are many types, or among many men, yet according to their parts, each is one. And they are completed in their individuals. For they are always divided according to what is theirs, and they are completed in a plural and manifold way. 

For this reason, looking at the Genus and the Species, what belongs to both? To the Genus, there shall be light <note>perhaps referring to the "illumination" or clarity a category provides</note> and many species. For the Genus always exists for the fulfillment of the Genus. 

<margin>learned</margin> 

The composite is always predicated of the species. And all those things that are higher <note>the "higher" genera in the hierarchy</note> are predicated of those below. But the **Species** is predicated neither of its neighbor nor of those above it. This is because it does not "reciprocate" <note>In logic, "reciprocation" or conversion means if A is B, then B is A. Here, it means while every man is an animal, not every animal is a man</note>. For it is always right and proper that the one which establishes the standing should be predicated [of the subject]. 

As the "neighing" is predicated of the horse, or the greater of the lesser: just as **Animal** is predicated of **Man**. But the lesser is no longer predicated of the greater; for you shall no longer say that an "Animal" is "Man," in the same way you said "Man" is an "Animal." However, for whatever things the species is predicated, of those same things the genus of that species must necessarily be predicated as well.

<summary>This page explores the logical relationship between Genus and Species, explaining that "Being" is not a single genus and detailing why higher categories can be predicated of lower ones, but not vice versa.</summary>

...and that is the **Species** <term>Species: *Eidos* in Greek; a group of things sharing a common nature under a larger genus</term> until the most individual stage. For it is true to say that a Lord is "loving of mankind," that a "man" is an **Animal** <term>Animal: *Kendani*; in logic, this refers to any living, sensing being</term>, and that an "animal" is a **Substance** <term>Substance: *Goyats'ut'yun*; the most basic category of being that exists in itself</term>. It is also true, though you say it less often, that a "man" is a "talking animal" and a "substance." **N**ow, among all those things predicated <note>Predicated: asserted or stated about a subject</note> from the highest levels, the lower levels and the species are predicated less than the individual. And the **Genus** <term>Genus: *Ser*; a broad category like "Animal" or "Plant"</term> is more generic than the individual and the species. Among those things that are "more," there are intermediate levels between each other, where the same thing can be both a species [to what is above] and a genus [to what is below] until the individual. **F**or just as the most generic genus contains everything under it—genera, species, and individuals—so the genus that is more specific, or the most specific itself, contains all the individual instances. The single species gathers together all the individuals <margin>° It gathers all the individuals together</margin> which are parts of it. And "individual" refers to **Socrates**, or "this white thing," or "this person who comes toward us, the son of Sophroniscus" <note>Sophroniscus was the historical father of the philosopher Socrates</note>, provided that Socrates is his only son. **N**ow, things are called **Individuals** <term>Individual: *Anhat*; literally "indivisible," referring to a single unique person or thing</term> because each one is composed of a unique collection of properties, the sum of which cannot exist in any other specific person. **F**or the specific properties of Socrates will not be exactly the same in any other specific person; however, regarding "Man," I say this is a common property...

<column-break/>

<page-num>8</page-num>
...which exists the same across many. One property is common to all individual men insofar as they are men. **B**ut the individual is contained by the species, and the species by the genus. For the genus is a kind of whole, and the individual is a part; the species is both a whole and a part. It is a part of another [the genus], and a whole not to another [genus], but to others [the individuals]. For it is complete in that way. **N**ow, concerning Genus and Species, what is "most generic," what is "most specific," what are the genera that are also species, what are individuals, and in how many ways "Genus" and "Species" are spoken of—all this has been said.

### Concerning Difference

**D**ifference <term>Difference: *Tarberut'yun*; the characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus</term> is spoken of in three ways: commonly, properly, and most properly. "Commonly," a thing is said to **Differ** from another when it is changed by any variation whatever, whether in relation to itself or to another. For Socrates differs from Plato by a variation, and he even differs from himself as a child compared to when he is a grown man, or when he is doing something compared to when he has ceased, and always as he has some change in his needs. And a thing is said to differ "properly" from another when it possesses an unvarying distinction, as when one differs from another by <gloss>because</gloss> an inseparable cause—such as a permanent scar, or the specific "hooked" shape of an aquiline nose <note>original: "արծու ընկնունութիւն" (artsu enknunut'yun) - refers to a nose shaped like an eagle's beak</note> fixed upon the face, or the actual features of the countenance.

### On Difference

...things are said to **differ** <term>Difference: *Tarberut’iwn* (Armenian) or *Differentia* (Latin); a characteristic that distinguishes one thing from another</term> from one another when they are distinguished by a specific production, such as a **man** from a **horse**. They are found to be distinguished by a specific difference, the **rational** <term>Rational: *Banakan*; possessing the faculty of reason</term> from the **irrational** <note>original: "khrakan" (խրական), usually rendered "anban" (անբան) for irrational in this context</note>. And because some differences are general, they make a thing "other" in a certain way, but in a common sense. In the same way, some make a thing "different." But in a specific sense, they are "other." For among differences, some make a thing "different" <note>original: "aylaylak" (այլայլակ), corresponding to the Greek *alloion*, referring to qualitative change or accidental difference</note> and some make it "other" <note>original: "ayl" (այլ), corresponding to the Greek *allos*, referring to an essential or specific difference</note>. Now, those that make a thing "other" are called **specific differences**. But those that make it "different" are simply called differences. For the difference of "animal" was taken for the "rational" [being]. But the species of "man" is "other" than the animal. Regarding movement, however, it is "different" only in a state of cessation. In this case, one is "other," while the other is "different" only in its manner of being. Now, according to these other productions, these divisions of the **Genus** <term>Genus: *Ser*; a general category like "Animal"</term> are essential. And definitions are explained from the Genus by such differences. But according to "difference" alone, a simple "otherness" consists only of having changes in itself. **N**ow, starting to speak again from the beginning: among differences, some are **separable** <term>Separable: *Anjatakan*; a quality that can change or be removed without destroying the subject, like being asleep</term> and some are **inseparable** <term>Inseparable: *Ananjateli*; a quality that cannot be removed, like being a rational creature</term>. For moving and resting, and being healthy and being sick, and as many things as are like these,

It is not a genus, nor a difference, nor a species, nor a property; yet it is always found existing within a subject.

A property is a characteristic that belongs only to one species, like "the ability to laugh" belongs only to humans.</note>. The property is **reciprocally predicated** <note>original: "հակասստորոգի" (hakas-storogi). ## Concerning the Common Traits of Genus and Accident

The Genus and the **accident** <note>original: "պատահումն" (patahmun). An accident is a characteristic that can come or go without changing what the thing is, like being "tan" or "sitting."</note> shall be spoken of generally as things predicated of others, as has been stated. This applies whether they are **separable** <note>e.g., sitting (you can stand up)</note> or **inseparable** <note>e.g., the blackness of a crow (it cannot be removed without the crow ceasing to be what it is)</note>. And since "movement" is predicated of other things, the genus is likewise spoken of in relation to animals and inanimate things.

## Concerning the Distinction Between Property and Accident

The genus is different from the accident: for the genus is prior to the species, whereas the accidents are posterior to the species. 

<column-break/>

<page-num>18</page-num>

For even if an accident is called "inseparable," the subject to which it happens is still prior to the accident itself. And the subjects receive the name along with the genus, but for the accident, it is not so. For accidents admit of **intensity and slackening** <note>original: "սաստկութի և թուղութի" (sastkut’i ew t’ułut’i). This refers to the logical concept of "more or less." You can be more or less "cold," but you cannot be more or less "human."</note>, whereas the genus does not. 

Furthermore, accidents exist primarily in individuals. However, the genera and the species are by nature prior to individual substances. And those [the genus and species] are predicated of what a thing is in its essence, whereas accidents are in the subject as "how" things are, or the quality of each. For as in a **crow** <note>A classic logical example: blackness is an inseparable accident of a crow.</note> you might say it is "black," regarding the "how" of **Socrates** <note>The famous Greek philosopher, often used as the "standard human" in logic textbooks.</note>, you might say he "sits" or "walks."

But while those things are differentiated from the others in four ways, as has been said, the accident is differentiated from those others in its own way by four types... <note>The final lines of the Armenian transcription appear fragmented or contain scribal abbreviations regarding the four-fold divisions of logic.</note> and each of them might be different... and there are many differences... and in the second, it is diminished by the difference taken for these.

<summary>This page compares "Property" and "Genus," explaining that properties are unique to one species while genera apply to many. It also introduces the "Accident," noting that while a Genus defines what a thing is, an Accident only describes how a thing is (quality) and can change in intensity.</summary>

When the difference of a thing was defined, it follows that how the property differs from the accident shall be discussed; and how it differs from the species, the difference, and the genus has been previously stated.

### Concerning the Common Traits of Difference and Species

It is to be accepted that **Difference** and **Species** are equally shared; for people receive the **rational** <note>original: "բանականն" (banakann). This is the 'Specific Difference' that defines a human.</note> trait equally according to their part, and they also receive the species. But it is common and always present in those who receive them, for **Socrates** is always rational, and Socrates is always a man.

### Concerning the Distinct Traits of Difference and Species

The **Difference** is predicated of "what kind" of thing it is <note>original: "որպիսի ինչ" (orpisi inch). In logic, the Difference describes the quality that distinguishes a species.</note>, while the **Species** is predicated of "what" the thing is <note>original: "զինչ են" (zinch en). The species describes the essential nature or 'essence' of the subject.</note>. For if "man" is predicated as a certain quality, it would not be a simple quality, but rather taken according to the underlying genus, and it would be a difference of the subjects. 

And this **difference** is seen over many species many times; for example, "rational" is seen over many species of living beings that are different in kind. But the **species** is only over those individuals which are of that specific form. 

Furthermore, the **difference** is prior to the species; for if you take away "rational," you also take away "man" <note>This is a classic logical principle: if you remove the defining characteristic (rationality), the species defined by it (human) can no longer exist.</note>.

Species <note>original: "Մասնակի" (masnaki) - literally 'particular' or 'species'</note> and property have in common that they are predicated of each other. For if something is a human, it is capable of laughter; and if it is capable of laughter, it is a human. This has been said many times. And in this way, there is a variety among those that receive the trait, and the property exists among those things for which they are proper.

## On the Similarity of Species and Property:

Species differs from property because a species can be predicated of others <note>i.e., a genus can be divided into many species</note>, while it is impossible for a property to belong to others <note>A property is unique to its specific species</note>. And the species exists as a subject before the property. But the property occurs in the species; for it is necessary for a human to be among those capable of laughter. And the species is always present in actuality <note>original: "ներգործութբ" (nerkortsut‘b) - referring to the Aristotelian concept of 'energeia' or being in action</note> in the subject. But the property is sometimes in potentiality <note>or "at rest"</note>; for a human is always "Socrates" in actuality, but "laughing" is not always in action, even though one is always naturally disposed to be "capable of laughter." There are those whose definitions are distinct and they themselves are distinct. I mean, the species is defined by the number of many differences... and it predicates *what things are* <note>In logic, this is 'quiddity'—the essence of a thing</note>. And as for such things as this: property exists in the single thing alone, and always in view...

...its new genus, it is common to be predicated of many... where there are other commonalities. Because there is a great deal of overlap between them... in the accident of those things that happened <note>The text is discussing 'accidents'—traits that are not essential to a definition</note>.

## On the Similarity of Species and Accident:

Property belongs to each; within the species, it predicates *what things are* <note>original: "զինչ են" (zinch en) - the 'whatness' or essence</note> for those of which it is the species. But the accident predicates *what sort* of thing it is, or *how it is* <note>Accidents describe qualities like color or size rather than the essential nature</note>. And each substance is capable of receiving a single species. But accidents are many, both separable and inseparable <note>A "separable" accident is something like "sitting" (you can stand up); an "inseparable" accident is something like "the blackness of a crow" (the crow is still a crow without it, but it never actually changes)</note>.
Species are understood before accidents, even if those accidents are inseparable. For it is necessary for the subject to exist so that something similar may happen to it. But accidents were naturally formed to be seen last... and they have a triple nature. Moreover, the species is received equally [by all members]; but the accident, even if it is inseparable, is not equal. For an Ethiopian <note>A classic logical example used by Porphyry to discuss inseparable accidents</note>, regarding the color of the Ethiopian, it might be newer or more intense according to [the individual].

Because property [is more] than species, and more than... and because it has been said to be more distinct.

...what intention lies behind the composition. Now, since many times, as we have said, the titles <note>original: "մակագրութիւնք" (makagrut'iwnk')—literally "inscriptions" or "superscriptions" at the head of a text.</note> are unreliable, for this reason, we require an investigation. of the compositions before us. Because many times, through deep compositions according to the mystery of the four modes—either due to the homonymy of the composition, which is twofold: either due to the homonymy of the composers, or due to the homonymy of the compositions themselves.

Regarding the homonymy of the composers: this is when two people are found who share the same name, and each writes compositions—some on the soul, and others on the heavens. In that case, because of the homonymy of the composers, no one can distinguish whose is whose, and both compositions are thought to belong to one man.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical introduction, transitioning from the methods of studying a text to the specific logical categories (the Five Universals) established by Porphyry and Aristotle. It focuses on the definition of "voice" or "sound" as the medium of philosophical expression.</meta>

<margin>
Concerning the classes.
</margin>
The civil order was arranged into fourteen stations; and just as Aristotle found all sensory things arranged into ten categories <term>storogut'iwnk'</term> <note>The "Categories" are Aristotle’s classification of everything that can be expressed: substance, quantity, quality, relation, etc.</note>, so too every philosophical "voice" <term>dzayn</term> <note>In ancient logic, "voice" (Greek: *phōnē*) refers to any meaningful or meaningless sound or spoken term.</note> is found arranged within these five [types]. For every philosophical voice is either a **genus**, a **species**, a **difference**, a **property**, or an **accident**. These voices are revealed through division, in this manner and according to this example:

"Voice" is twofold: it is either articulate <note>original: "yardeal" — literally "joined" or "composed"</note> or inarticulate <note>original: "anyard" — "unjoined"</note>. An articulate voice is like that of a human, while an inarticulate one is like that of animals or the clanging of inanimate objects. And each of these is again twofold: either significant or insignificant.

An articulate significant voice is like the "goat-stag" <note>original: "arcup'enjn iros," a corruption of the Greek *tragelaphos* or Latin *hircocervus*—a mythical creature used in logic to show a word can have meaning without a physical reality.</note>, because it is composed of syllables and signifies a stag with the features of a goat. However, an articulate insignificant voice is like "blituri" <note>original: "chiakhay kin" / "blitri" — "Blituri" was a standard nonsense word used by ancient logicians to demonstrate a sound that is articulate but lacks meaning.</note> or "scindapsus." For although these are articulate, they do not signify anything.

An inarticulate and significant voice is like the barking of a dog; for although it is inarticulate, it signifies the arrival of a man or a beast. But an inarticulate and insignificant voice is like a cough or a mere thumping sound.

<meta>The transcription "բ. հնձ...ե" appears to be a marginal or gutter note, possibly a reference to a specific section or an abbreviated owner's mark.</meta>

<column-break/>

<page-num>22</page-num>
In this way, philosophers do not employ the inarticulate voice, nor the articulate but insignificant sound like "blituri." Instead, they employ that which is articulate and significant. Among articulate significant voices, there is a twofold division: either **universal** <note>original: "hanur"</note> or **particular** <note>original: "masnakan"</note>.

A particular voice is like "Socrates." A universal voice is like "man," "horse," or "eagle." Philosophers do not use the particular voice because particulars are indefinite <note>Science and philosophy, in the Aristotelian tradition, deal with general truths rather than individual instances.</note>, but they use the universal voice. And this, being articulate and significant, is again twofold: it is either **substance** <term>eghust</term> <note>An archaic Armenian term for "being" or "essence," corresponding to the Greek *ousia*.</note> or **accident** <term>makeghust</term> <note>Literally "that which stands upon being"; the Armenian equivalent of the Greek *symbebēkos*.</note>.

Regarding "accident": every accident is that which occurs to a color or a thing and has a twofold existence. For an accident is twofold: it belongs either to one nature or to many. If it belongs to a multitude, it is an "accident" proper, which is twofold: **separable** and **inseparable**.

A **separable accident** is like "sitting" or "working" <note>One can stop sitting without ceasing to be human.</note>. An **inseparable accident** is like the "blackness of a crow" or "snub-nosedness." When it belongs to only one nature, it is a **property** <term>yatuk</term>. This is an accident belonging to one nature, <margin>What does it belong to?</margin> such as when we say "the ability to laugh" is a property of humans. And this, being a substance, is again twofold: for it belongs either to one nature or to many. And if it belongs to many natures...

The superficial is that which, whether it is present or absent, does not destroy or constitute the substance, such as "whiteness" in a person.

### Concerning the nature of "What is it?"

In the establishment of the following composition, we shall come to the purpose and the utility. If those things are necessary for this composition, they are threefold. For the purpose of the present composition is Aristotle’s *Categories* <term>Storogut'iwnk'</term>, from which comes all philosophy and the methods of logic. And the utility of Aristotle’s *Categories* is this: Aristotle teaches us regarding the ten "most generic" genera. And in this present composition, we learn what a genus is; and again, how these genera are threefold and are divided into species by means of differences. For example, "animal" being a genus, it is divided into species by means of differences—namely, "rational" and "irrational." This present composition teaches us what a species is and what a distinction is.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of logic, moving from specific types of reasoning (induction and paradigms) to the systematic hierarchy of the four logical methods: division, definition, demonstration, and analysis. ...the four elements and placed them into each species from which they are composed. But let us speak of their arrangement. The goal is to know that the method of **division** <term>bazhanakan</term> precedes that of **definition** <term>sahmanakan</term>, because division naturally comes before the definition. For anyone who wishes to define something useful must complete the definition starting from division.

Furthermore, the definitional precedes the **demonstrative** <term>apats’uts’akan</term>. For as Aristotle says, "the beginning of demonstration is the definition." This is because demonstration always presents the nature of the subjects under consideration, whereas the definition reveals that nature.

Finally, the **analytical** <term>verlutsakan</term> <note>Analysis in this context refers to the process of breaking down a complex proposition or syllogism into its simplest components.</note> was placed last, because analysis has an inverse relationship to division. For division starts from the simplest parts and proceeds to the composite whole; conversely, analysis begins with the composite and ends at the simplest components. Here, definition and demonstration are also related; for those that enter into many natures, analysis further divides them into many parts. Knowing these things, let us now join them to how they are useful for the present composition. The goal is to know how the method of division

<column-break/>

is useful in this way: just as we see in other things, those who divide create a certain connection of form. For example, in the animal kingdom, the genus <note>original: "azgn," usually meaning 'nation' or 'race', here used for genus.</note>, the wood, and the limbs are divided within the wood. Likewise here, there is that which divides, that which is divided, and those into which the division occurs.

That which is divided here is the **genus** <term>ser</term>. Those that perform the division are the **constitutive differences** <term>baghkats’uts’ich’ zanazanut’iwn</term> <note>These are the specific characteristics that distinguish one species from another within the same genus.</note>. And those into which the division was made are the **species** <term>tesak</term>.

Since division naturally proceeds from the genus into species by means of constitutive differences, this composition is useful to us because it teaches what a genus is, what a species is, and what constitutive differences are.

At the start, the definitional method is useful because a definition is composed of a genus and constitutive differences. Take, for example, the definition of **Man**: "animal, rational, mortal, capable of mind and genius <note>original: "hancharoy," often translated as intellect or talent.</note>." Here, "animal" is the genus, and the others are the constitutive differences, which this present composition teaches us. If it is useful for the definitional, then it is also useful for the demonstrative, because as we said before, the beginning of demonstration is the definitional.

# The Utility and Intention of Philosophy

Having divided the **utility** <term>pitanats’u</term> into two parts, he placed the **intention** <term>ditaworut’iun</term> between them. For the intention itself draws us toward the subject. For according to **Plato** <note>original: "Platoni." The author cites Plato’s famous dictum from the *Theaetetus* that philosophy begins in wonder.</note>, "The one true beginning of thinking is to know what the object of thought is." Without this, one would necessarily go astray in all things. 

For he who is ignorant of the intention of the upcoming composition will not be able to follow the things spoken to their proper completion. But **utility** is said to draw us toward itself; for by finding the utility of the upcoming composition through proper means, we are encouraged. However, he who is ungracious toward the beginning of wisdom should know that it is a divine honor to seek knowledge. 

For he who **wonders** <note>original: "skanch’anawor."</note> falls into inquiry by that very act. And if one does not fall into inquiry, they are called sluggish. A person is praised when they see the divine arrangement of the three-sided <note>Likely referring to a triangle or a geometric representation of logic.</note> creation and wonders what it is. If they see the mixture of various colors at the end of a thing and do not fall into inquiry, they gain nothing. But if they wonder, then they fall into inquiry; and then they undertake to practice **philosophy** <term>imastasirel</term>. Therefore, one must begin with utility, because, as we said, through wonder, utility becomes the beginning of philosophy.

<meta>This page continues the logical analysis of Porphyry’s Introduction, specifically examining the order of the "Five Voices" (Genus, Difference, Species, Property, and Accident). It transitions from the general utility of philosophy to the specific classification of beings into universals and particulars.</meta>

...being is rational <note>The text likely concludes a sentence about the definition of man as a "rational animal."</note>. But it must be **ASKED**: 
<margin>fourth rank</margin>
**WHY** did he first rank the **genus** <term>ser</term>, second the **difference** <term>tarberut’iun</term>, third the **species** <term>tesak</term>, then the **property** <term>yatuk</term> and the **accident** <term>patahumun</term>? But before giving the answer, we must note that among beings, some are **particular** and some are **universal**. Now, it is the nature of particulars—those with specific forms—that they are not always the same nor do they exist in a fixed way; however, universals are naturally disposed to be always and in the same way. And so it is that **philosophy** <term>imastasirut’iun</term> finds its firm foundation in those things which are naturally disposed to be always and in the same way. But with the particulars, which are called **individuals** <note>original: "masnaturk," meaning those things given as parts or individuals.</note>, philosophy does not concern itself with their endless variety. And these individuals are like **Socrates**, **Plato**, and **Alcibiades**, who are also called "indivisibles" <term>anhatk</term>. They are called indivisibles <note>The Armenian "anhat" literally means "uncut" or "undivided," translating the Greek "atomos."</note> because if they are divided, they cannot preserve their original species. For if one divides a whole person into parts, those parts no longer preserve the form of the whole. And because universals are more honorable, as they exist always and in the same way, for this reason **Porphyry** <note>Porphyry of Tyre (c. 234–305 AD), a Neoplatonist whose "Introduction" (Isagoge) to Aristotle's logic became a standard textbook in the Middle Ages.</note> first ranked the genus among the universals, followed by the difference and the species. For whatever is rational, which is a **difference**, is also 

<column-break/>

an animal, which is the **genus**; but not every animal is also rational <note>In traditional logic, "Animal" is a broader category (genus) than "Rational" (the difference that defines humans).</note>. Now, because the genus is more universal than the difference, and thereby provides a broader foundation, for this reason he placed it first. Furthermore, he placed **difference** before **species** for the same reason; because difference is more universal than species. For whatever is "man," which is the **species**, is also "rational," which is the **difference**; but not everything rational is necessarily a man <note>The author may be considering angels or other rational beings in a theological context.</note>. For this reason, difference was ranked before species. At the beginning, he ranked species before **property**. This is because species pertains to the **essence** <term>yeghuat</term> <note>original: "yeghuat," an archaic term for "essence" or "substance."</note>, while property is a resulting **accident**. The essence is more foundational than that which is merely a resulting attribute. Regarding this, some might raise an objection, saying that a property is sometimes found in the essence, such as being "capable of laughter" <note>A classic example in ancient logic: only humans (the species) have the "property" of laughter.</note>. Why then did he rank species before the essential property? To resolve this doubt, we say that because the species is *always* essential, whereas a property is not always just essential but can also be an attribute. For this reason, he ranked the "always essential" before the "resulting essence." Finally, he ranked **property** before **accident**, because a property is something that stems from the nature of the thing—such as being capable of learning or wisdom—whereas an **accident** is...

<summary>This page explains the hierarchical ordering of Porphyry's five logical categories, arguing that broader universals (like Genus) must precede more specific ones (like Species) because they are more "honorable" and foundational to philosophy.</summary>

# Of the many essential things, which is the principal.

Here some people are in doubt as to why he placed the **essential** <term>karevor</term> <note>original: "karevor." In this context, it refers to things that are "necessary" or "essential" to a definition.</note> first. We answer: Although it is proper to begin with the universals, **Porphyry** <note>The 3rd-century philosopher whose textbook on logic is being discussed.</note>, thinking the same, made this the beginning. Now, the "essential" is spoken of in many ways, and it must be known that these two names are joined to one another. 

<margin>the useful</margin>
But the **useful** <term>pitanatsun</term> is divided into two: the **like-good** and the **essential**. The "good" is that which is chosen for its own sake, such as **piety** <term>barepashtut'iun</term> or a good reputation. But the "useful" is distinguished from the **essential**. An **accident** <note>The text uses a term related to "chance" or "occurrence."</note> is that which, when present, does not create the substance, and when absent, does not destroy it. Such as this

---

thing, or that which accompanies it, or that which is born by will. But the **essential** is that which, when present, creates the substance, and when absent, destroys it. For example, it is essential for the "six voices" <note>The commentator may be adding a sixth category or referring to a specific arrangement of the five.</note> to exist. Or as the builder is to the ship, his craftsmanship is essential to it. Or as a **difference** <term>zanazanut’iun</term>; as when we say it is essential for a human to have **rationality** <term>banakanut’iun</term>. 

Or it is used in the sense of force <note>compulsion</note>, as when we say: it is essential <note>necessary</note> to flee from what is harmful, that is to say, "by necessity." And it is used as a consequence, as when we say: the conclusion **essentially** <note>logically</note> follows the premise.

But he calls it "essential" when it is something to be avoided, yet chosen for the sake of another. For example: **bloodletting** <note>original: "eraku hatn," literally "the cutting of a vein."</note>. For the lancet is to be avoided for its own sake <note>because it causes pain</note>, but it is chosen for the sake of causing a recovery, and for the sake of **health** <term>aroghjut’iun</term>. It is called essential when one thing is chosen for another, like health. For health is considered a gift for something else, namely for the activities of nutrition. For never, they say, can the personal actions of the soul proceed without health. And in this last sense, it is said to be essential for the structure of the household...

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of Porphyry’s *Isagoge*. Having introduced Porphyry's pedagogical strategy on the previous page—specifically his decision to bypass complex metaphysical debates—the commentator now explores the specific philosophical questions Porphyry declined to answer: whether "universals" (the Five Voices) exist in reality or only in the mind.</meta>

<margin>1</margin> regarding these voices: whether they exist, or whether they do not exist;
<margin>2</margin> whether they exist by intellectual conception alone, or whether they are 
<margin>3</margin> subsisting [in reality]; and what an "intellectual conception" is. 

We shall say: an "intellectual conception" <term>makanmtatsut’iwn</term> <note>This term refers to a secondary mental construction or a concept formed by the mind, often distinguishing between things that exist in nature and things the mind "builds."</note> is that whose origin is found in discursive reasoning <term>tramakhohut’iwn</term>, but it possesses a corruption of our mind. This occurs when someone, in their reasoning, forms a mental concept of a **stag-goat** <note>original: "yeghjerus arashn." This is a classic philosophical example (the Greek *tragelaphos*) of a creature that can be imagined but does not exist in nature.</note>, which nature did not create. Instead, our mental conception forces the nature of our perceptions toward a certain living thing—combining a deer and a goat—which nature does not know. By remembering this, the mental conception creates a "becoming," but it is a corruption of the mind.

However, the "substantial" <note>The text uses "ent’akayakan," meaning that which underlies or acts as a subject.</note> is that which nature created and knows: such as a **man**, a **horse**, or an **eagle**, which do not have their origin in mere intellectual conception. 

Now, he said well that "I do not seek whether these living voices exist or do not exist," so that I might not enter into the **deepest inquiries**, and so that one might not be distracted from the common [teachings]. For what does one need of such inquiries? Is there perhaps some doubt regarding the existence or non-existence of these five voices? We say: if there was doubt among the ancient logicians whether they exist—since indeed in the...

<column-break/>

...the mind, they see "humanity." In truth, our skill is not hereditary, but is a discipline. Making this clear: if indeed the things perceived by the senses exist, while the universal and wise things do not, we say in opposition: not everything that exists falls under sense perception. For if only those things which fall under sense perception are "beings," then it follows that the incorporeal, the mind, and the soul—which do not fall under sense perception—are therefore not beings. 

Furthermore, I must not even trust the senses themselves, for they do not grasp much of the truth. The **sun**, being many times larger than the earth, is seen only as the **size of a span** <note>A "span" is the distance from the thumb to the little finger; the text argues that senses deceive us about the true scale of the cosmos.</note>. And the **oar** of a boat is seen by the senses as "broken" in the water <note>The classic "bent oar" illusion used by skeptics and philosophers to show that senses can be misleading.</note>. 

But having shown that you unfairly cast aside the most indestructible canonical [rules], let us say what the "universal" is. The **Universal** is: "one in number, received by many according to species." Now, we said "one in number" because it is a single thing. And because it is also a thing of antiquity <note>or "nature/essence" (hnut’iwn/p’nut’iwn)</note>, we said "according to species." For though nature is one thing, it is not so merely by species. And what the universal is as "matter," and its "nature," and what comes before and after, we shall see together in the art of rhetoric <note>original: "eresabanut’ean," likely referring to the study of perspectives or "prosopography" in a logical context.</note>.

...place of instruction. But if it is received and believed by the many, it is because it exists in many parts. And we shall say how it is one while being in many parts. <meta>This page continues the logical investigation into the nature of universals, shifting from the general definition of a "species" to a specific debate between ancient schools of thought—namely the Pythagoreans and the Stoics—regarding whether concepts like "Humanity" or "Animal" are physical bodies or incorporeal relations.</meta>

...because he subdues the dim war of the broad King. Now, problems and doubts arose among the ancients regarding constitutive and defining statements. First, the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who often explained the universe through numbers and geometric proportions.</note> said that every incorporeal thing is structured according to a triple dimension <note>Likely referring to length, breadth, and depth.</note>. First and foremost, he considers it best to follow the **Aristotelian** distinctions. In the matter of **homonyms** <term>original: "homanunut‘iwn" (հոմանունութիւն). First: in how many senses are we using the term? Second: regarding which specific sense is the present discussion? And third: to predicate and define that which the discourse is about. If one does not wish to follow these distinctions, they will fall into infinite ambiguity; indeed, they will be lost, for homonymy is the mother of error and doubt. 

But as the master of distinctions, the excellent **Porphyry** <note>The OCR reads "zarphiophos" (զարփիոփոս), a common scribal corruption or phonetic rendering of the name "Porphyrios" (Պորփիւրոս).</note> first and foremost distinguishes the homonyms and states in how many senses the term is used. <meta>This page continues the logical commentary on Porphyry's Isagoge, specifically dissecting the definitions of the Five Universals. ...what is man? The answer would be: "we are rational," which is the **difference**. <note>In logic, the "difference" is the specific trait that separates one species from others in the same genus.</note> If asked "what sort of thing [are we]?" we answer: "capable of laughter," which is a **property**. <term>original: "yatuk" (յատուկ). It must be known that they are called "intermediate" because they are capable of being both **genus** and **species**: a **species** of that which is [higher] than it, and a **genus** to those [lower] than it.

Now, having determined what is the "most generic" and what is the "most specific," and what the intermediates are, let us bring forth the technical division <note>original: "arhest-teghakan" (արհեստտեղական). This likely refers to the systematic logical method of *division* used to define terms.</note> concerning these things, so that we may learn the most accurate truth. Now, the masters of logic divide the **most generic genus** in this way: **Substance** <term>Substance: the primary category of that which exists in itself</term> is divided into **Body** and **Incorporeal**. **Body** is divided into **Animate** and **Inanimate**. **Animate** is divided into the **Zoophyte** <term>Zoophyte: literally "animal-plant," a creature like a sponge or coral that appears to belong to both kingdoms</term> and the... and into the **Ani-**

<column-break/>

**-mal**. **Animal** is divided into **Rational** and **Irrational**. **Rational** is divided into **Mortal** and **Immortal**. **Mortal** is divided into... 

Now, they call **Substance** the **most generic genus** <note>Latin: *Summum Genus*</note> because it has many genera surpassing it <note>This refers to Substance being the "top" category with no genus above it.</note>. But they call **Man** the **most specific species** <note>Latin: *Infima Species*</note> because there is no other species below it; for this is the final term. However, they call **Animal** and **Animate** "intermediate genera" and "intermediate species," because by being in the middle, they are capable of being both genus and species.

These things are as follows. Now let us recount what **Animal**, **Zoophyte**, and **Plant** are. Now, the **Plant** is the lowest [form of life], which possesses three distinctions: the **procreative** <note>original: "tsnndakan" (ծննդական). The faculty of reproduction.</note>, the **augmentative** (growth), and the **nutritive**. And because it is in the nature of the Creator to grant us life, He granted the procreative and the augmentative faculties; so that, once growth is complete, the being might be able to bear its like. And because the augmentative faculty has need of the nutritive, for this reason He also granted us the nutritive faculty.

Now, by receiving one additional faculty along with these three—that is, the **sensory** <term>sensory: the ability to perceive through the senses</term>—it becomes a **zoophyte**. And the reason why the zoophyte possesses only the sense of **touch** is clear: for when the sun rises over the sea, the oyster <note>original: "kochghan" (կոճղան). Likely refers to a bivalve or mollusk.</note> opens its shell and... <note>original: "keshtanumay" (կեշտանումայ). An obscure term likely referring to a specific marine creature.</note>, and when the light strikes it, it retracts.

### On the Division of Being and the Hierarchy of Nature

->**The Division of the Whole**<-

But in those things which are named differently <note>original: "annmananun" (աննմանանուն). In logic, this refers to heteronyms—things that have different names and different definitions, like the parts of a body.</note>, such as **Socrates**—his hands and his head—they are not divided the same way. However, **Being** <term>Being: "ēak" (էակ), the most fundamental category of existence in philosophy</term> in its most generic genus is not divided like a "similar part" of them. For those things consisting of similar parts <note>referring to "homoeomerous" substances like water or gold, where every part is the same as the whole</note> share both the name and the nature of the thing they are named after. 

But the most generic genera, although they share the name of **Being**, do not share the nature [identically]. Nor can it be divided in an entirely similar way. For those things divided into dissimilar parts share neither the name nor the nature. But the most generic genera, although they differ in nature, nonetheless share the name; for they are all called "beings." 

<margin>
+ Accidents <term>Accidents: "patahmunk‘" (պատահմունք), properties that can change without destroying the essence (like being tan or sitting)</term> rather than Being are the only certain ones; however, from this it is also certain that the number is 4.
</margin>

But [Being] is not divided like a homonymous sound <note>original: "hamanun" (համանուն), meaning "equivocal." Like the word "bank" (river bank vs. money bank), which shares a name but has different meanings.</note>; for the homonym involves a sharing of the name only. In contrast, **Being** provides a sharing of both the name and the nature to the most generic genera. 

Secondly, a homonymous sound is shared equally, but **Being** is not shared this way among the most generic genera. For **Substance** <term>Substance: "goyac‘ut‘iwn" (գոյացութիւն), that which exists in itself and not in another</term> is "more" of a being than the others. Accidents are "lesser" in existence. ->**On Priority and Sequence**<-

But let us speak of what is "first by nature," and "later," or "last." That which is **first by nature** is that which entails <term>entails: "šaraberi" (շարաբերի), meaning "if X exists, then Y must also exist"</term> but is not [necessarily] entailed. For example: **Animal** is "first by nature." For whenever you say "Man," "Animal" is entailed—that is to say, he is an animal. But when you say "Animal," "Man" is not [necessarily] entailed; for not everything that is once an animal is a man.

And although he promised to follow the present matters of philosophy, yet he does not entirely leave without mention the command of the teacher—that is to say, **Plato**. For Plato transmits to us **three modes of division** <term>Division: "bažanumn" (բաժանումն), referring to the logical method of *diairesis* used to define a concept</term>, of which the first is this: he says that it is necessary to place the division from the **most generic genera** <term>Most generic: "seṙakanaguyn" (սեռականագոյն), the highest level of classification like "Substance"</term> down to the **most specific species** <term>Most specific: "tesakaguyn" (տեսակագոյն), the lowest level of species that cannot be divided further, such as "Human"</term>. And one must not pass beyond those most specific species. 

It is to be asked why he commands to descend to the most specific species and not to pass beyond them into **individuals** <term>Individuals: "anhat" (անհատ), literally "indivisible," referring to singular things like "this person"</term>. And we say that for this reason he does not command passing into individuals: lest the division fall into singulars which do not possess **eternity** <note>original: "mštnǰenaworut‘iwn" (մշտնջենաւորութիւն). In this context, it refers to universal stability or permanence. Science and logic deal with the "eternal" universal, not the "transient" individual.</note>. For if you say that "Man" is divided into **Socrates**, into **Plato**, and into other various mixed and transient <unclear>physicalities</unclear>, [you depart from science]. But in those [divisions] which ought to be [constant], there is no further decrease; for it is necessary for a division to be eternal [universal]. As when **Substance** <term>Substance: "goyac‘ut‘iwn" (գոյացութիւն)</term> is divided into the corporeal and the incorporeal, and into the living and into 

<column-break/>

the rational, and so forth. For firm knowledge exists according to eternal things and those which always exist in the same way. Others say that it is necessary for the division not to result in such and such individuals—that is, **Astghik** <note>Astghik is a common Armenian name used here as a placeholder for a generic individual, much like "John Doe."</note> or **Asclepiades** <note>original: "Yałepiad" (Յաղեպիադ), the Armenian transliteration of the Greek name Asclepiades.</note>—but into the universal and the [species]. To this we say that the universal word is nothing else but the species of the most specific species.

The **second mode of division** which Plato commands to observe says that it is necessary, when you divide, not to confuse the division by skipping over superior steps <note>This refers to the rule against "jumping" in a logical hierarchy, such as moving from "Animal" to "Socrates" without passing through "Human."</note>, but to move in order. First proposition: Humans are living beings.
And the second proposition: The living being exists.
A proposition contains a **subject** <term>Subject: "ent'akay" (ենթակայ). Literally "that which lies under"; the primary noun or topic being discussed.</term> and a **predicate** <term>Predicate: "storogyal" (ստորոգեալ). Literally "that which is spoken down"; the quality or category attributed to the subject.</term>. 
In the first proposition, the subject is "human," while the predicate is "living being."
In the second proposition, the subject is "living being," and the predicate is "exists."
Now, the predicate must either be more extensive <note>meaning it covers a broader category</note> than the subject, or equal to it.
But it is never less. The subject is either equal or less, but never more than the predicate.
The predicate is more extensive than the subject, just as "living being" is broader than "human." But we say a predicate is "equal" to a subject regarding its specific properties; for example, for a human, the "ability to laugh" <note>In classical logic, being "capable of laughter" was considered a unique property of humans, making the two terms interchangeable or "convertible."</note>. The quality of "laughing" and "human" possess a similarity and are reversible.
And from those things previously mentioned, the primary division is as follows: **substance** <term>Substance: "goyats'ut'yun" (գոյացութիւն). The essential nature of a thing that exists in itself.</term> is only a predicate <note>This refers to Substance as the highest genus in the Tree of Porphyry; it is predicated of everything below it.</note>,
<margin>⋮</margin>while **individuals** <term>Individuals: "anhatk'" (անհատք). The specific, indivisible examples of a species, like a specific person.</term> are subjects. 
<margin>⋮</margin>But the middle categories,

are both predicates and subjects.
In the more familiar [particular] case, the subject is more prominent than the predicate, for their confirmation is predicated of them; but being the "underlying" things, they are distinct and define the recurrences.
However, the middle predicates are more extensive than the subjects. From this, a doubt arises for the learner: "How can you say substance is a predicate? For we see the opposite with the color white. White itself is an **accident** <term>Accident: "patahum" (պատահումն). A non-essential property (like color or size) that can change without the thing ceasing to be what it is.</term> predicated of substance, and is not substance itself; white is an accident."
The respondent says: You are right to say substance is a subject, for it is also the subject for individual accidents.
But to this we say: we do not mean that [substance] is predicated of everything, but only of those things defined by it. For those things defined by it [the species and individuals under it], it is never a subject but always a predicate.
As an example of what was said, let us apply the same division: substance shall be like a "whole," and individuals like "parts." The middle categories are both wholes and parts.
In the more familiar [particular individuals], they are more like parts than wholes. In the opposites [the highest categories], they are more like wholes than parts.

Now, just as the **whole** contains its entirety within its parts, so too does **substance** <term>Substance: "goyats'ut'i" (գոյացութիւն). # On Difference

Now, beginning the teaching concerning **Difference** <term>Difference: "tarberut'yun" (տարբերութիւն). In logic, this refers to the characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus.</term>, we must first define it according to the clarity established by **Aristotle**, specifically how we should distinguish it from **homonyms** <term>Homonym: "homanun" (հոմանուն). Words that sound the same but have different meanings.</term>. For within the sound of a homonym, there are differences.

Now, first, **Difference** is threefold: for Difference is spoken of **commonly**, **specially**, and **most specifically**.
1. **Commonly**: That which signifies various **accidents** <margin>accident</margin>.
2. **Specially**: That which signifies various **separable accidents**.
3. **Most Specifically**: That which alters the **substance** <term>Substance: "goyats'ut'yun" (գոյացութիւն). The essential nature of a thing.</term> itself.

For example, a man may happen to be blue-eyed or black-eyed. Being blue-eyed is a **separable accident** <note>original: "anjatakan" (անջատական). An attribute that can change without changing the nature of the person.</note> for the first man, while being black-eyed may be an **inseparable accident** for the second. Or perhaps one has a scar—this is a separable black mark. 

But regarding the third kind [Most Specific]: it is the **rational** <note>original: "banakan" (բանական). From "ban" (word/reason), equivalent to the Greek "logikos".</note>, which distinguishes us holily from the **irrational** <note>Animals or beings without reason.</note>. This difference reveals the very **substance**.

But one must ask: why are there exactly **three** differences, and not more or fewer? It is right to speak of this with certainty at the end: why did they happen to be thus? 

There are two realities: either **accident** or **substance**. 
If it is an **accident**, it is either **separable** or **inseparable**. 
Now, if it is **separable**,
<meta>catchword: separable</meta>

<column-break/>

it carries the **common accident**. 
But if it is **inseparable**, it carries the **special accident**. 
And if it involves **substance**, it creates the **most specific difference**, such as **rational** and **mortal**, which are the constituents of substance.

Thus, if there are three realities, they are divided rightly into three types of Difference. 

The second reason is what the **Holy Philosopher** <note>Likely referring to David the Invincible (Davit' Anhaght'), a 6th-century Neoplatonist Armenian philosopher who commented extensively on Porphyry and Aristotle.</note> says: substance is **"Other"** <note>original: "ayl" (այլ). Refers to a difference in kind or essence.</note>, while accident is **"Altered"** <note>original: "aylayluk" (այլայլակ). Refers to a change in state or quality within the same essence.</note>. The following composition teaches us how substance is one thing and accident is another. 

Now, when one marvels at these things, one makes two pairings: one "other" that is **separable**, and one "other" that is **inseparable**; one "altered" that is **separable**, and one "altered" that is **inseparable**. There are two more: "other" and "altered" in the **separable**, and the same in the **inseparable**. This makes **six** combinations. 

And of these six, three are coherent <note>original: "baghkanan" (բաղկանան). Meaning they logically consist or hold together.</note>, and three are not. Those that are coherent are those that correspond with one another, pertaining to the state of being. Those that are not coherent are the opposites.
